t1-1.what:
Definition: Component API design means defining a component's public contract: which props it takes, what they are called, which are required, which have defaults, and what it deliberately does not offer.

In a design round the interviewer's first question is usually "What will its API be?" Don't answer with a list of props. Answer with your reasoning: which data is essential, which is optional, and where the consumer needs control.
t1-1.analogy: A restaurant menu. A short menu means every dish comes out well. A 200-item menu confuses the kitchen and quality drops. A component works the same way: a small, clean API is more reliable.
t1-1.why:
Once an API is public, changing it is a breaking change. In a design system, renaming one prop can mean refactoring 200 files. That is why interviewers want to see that you think ahead.

The most common mistake is adding a new boolean prop for every new requirement: isBig, isRed, hasIcon, showBorder. Six months later you have 22 props and most combinations make no sense. The fix is variant + composition.
pros: A union variant makes impossible combinations unrepresentable
...rest forwards native props for free
A small API means fewer breaking changes and less documentation
cons: Cases with only a "tiny difference" are awkward to express as variants
An escape hatch (className) can erode the design system's consistency
Composition takes longer to learn, and props feel more obvious at first
gotchas: In a design round, state the API first and the implementation later. That is what the interviewer is waiting for
Decide deliberately whether ...rest goes before or after your own props, because that determines which side wins
Use a boolean prop only when the value is truly binary. For three or more states, use a string union
terms: everything about a component that outside code can use, mainly its props
a prop that lets the consumer step outside the default behavior (className, render)
adding a new prop for every new requirement until a component has 20 of them
where: Button, Input, Card: components that hundreds of developers use
the answer to "What will its API be?" starts here
the public contract of an npm package

// ...rest is ESSENTIAL -- aria-*, data-*, onFocus all pass through
SAHI -- union variants + composition + escape hatch
CORRECT -- union variants + composition + escape hatch

t1-2.what:
Definition: In a design interview, just saying "controlled vs uncontrolled" is not enough. Support both. The production standard is: if the value prop is provided, the component is controlled; if not, it keeps its own state, starting from defaultValue.

Every good library does this: Radix, MUI, React Aria, and others.
t1-2.analogy: Cruise control in a car. Sometimes you want to press the accelerator yourself (controlled); sometimes you want the car to hold its speed on its own (uncontrolled). Offering only one of the two is a rigid design.
t1-2.why:
In about 90% of use cases, the consumer doesn't care about the value; they just need a working dropdown. Forcing all of them to be controlled means a pointless useState everywhere. The other 10% (using a form library, or syncing the value with the URL) really do need control.

The hybrid pattern serves both. If you wrap it in a useControllableState hook, you can reuse it across the whole design system.
pros: The simple case stays simple while the complex case is still possible
One hook is reused across the whole design system
onChange fires in both modes, so analytics and validation keep working
cons: Each component needs a little extra code
Bugs can appear if the mode switches mid-lifecycle
You have to explain the reasoning behind both branches to the interviewer
gotchas: If value goes from undefined to defined, the component has switched from uncontrolled to controlled. Always add a dev warning
Call onChange in uncontrolled mode too, otherwise the consumer is left blind
Do NOT update internal state in controlled mode, or you end up with two sources of truth
terms: the value comes from the parent's state
the component manages its own value
supports both: controlled if a value is provided, internal state otherwise
where: React Hook Form often needs the component to be controlled
drive a filter or tab from the URL

t1-3.what:
Definition: A compound component holds shared state in a parent and passes it to its children through Context. The consumer writes it almost like HTML: <Tabs><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab/></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel/></Tabs>.

In a design round this is your answer on flexibility, for example when the interviewer asks "what if the client wants a divider between tabs?"
t1-3.why:
A config-object API (<Tabs items={[...]} />) is fine while the layout is fixed. As soon as the first custom requirement arrives (a badge on a tab, a divider, tabs at the bottom), you have to add yet another prop. With a compound component the layout belongs to the consumer, and you only provide the behaviour: state, keyboard handling, ARIA.

That is why Radix and Headless UI are built this way. They ship behaviour, not looks.
pros: The consumer has full control over layout
Prop explosion goes away
Behaviour (keyboard, ARIA) lives in one place and every consumer gets it for free
cons: The dependency is implicit, so using a part in the wrong place causes a runtime error
Too much boilerplate for small widgets
Dot-notation types in TypeScript take a bit of extra work
gotchas: Check for a null Context and throw a clear error. It beats "cannot read property of null"
Don't inspect children with React.Children.map. It breaks as soon as a wrapper appears in between
Memoize the Context value with useMemo, otherwise every tab re-renders on each render
terms: several components that together form one widget
parent state that children receive automatically through Context
a place where the consumer can insert their own content
where: the core pattern behind Radix and Headless UI

If the interviewer asks "what if we need X?", the compound answer is "yes, just write it"

t1-4.what:
Definition: There are two ways to make a component flexible:

  • Configuration: <Card title icon actions showBorder />. Simple, but every new case needs a new prop.
  • Composition: <Card><Card.Header/><Card.Body/></Card>. More code to write, but unlimited flexibility.

The middle path is slots: <Card header={<X/>} footer={<Y/>} />.
t1-4.why:
A rule of thumb that works well in interviews: "Config for data, composition for structure." Anything that is data (title text, disabled) stays a prop. Anything that is structure (where things appear and how) should come from children or a slot.

A bonus people often forget: composition also gives a performance benefit. Children are created outside the parent, so when the parent's state changes, their element reference stays the same and React skips re-rendering them.
pros: A new requirement doesn't need a new prop
Composition gives a free performance benefit
The component's own code stays small
cons: Call sites become verbose
Structure isn't enforced, so consumers can put anything inside
Simple cases can feel over-engineered
gotchas: Saying "config for data, composition for structure" in an interview lands well
Slots (ReactNode props) are the middle path: fixed structure with flexible content
Mention the performance benefit of children as props. Very few candidates know it
terms: building a larger component by combining small pieces
describing everything about a component through props
a named prop that receives JSX, such as header, footer or actions
where: separating a wrapper's state from a heavy child

t1-5.what:
Definition: Keep state only as high as it needs to be, and no higher. The default is at the bottom; lift it up only when two siblings both need it.

In a design round this is the first answer for performance, before memo.
t1-5.analogy: Household items. Keep the tea cup in the kitchen, not in the storage room. Something used in only one room shouldn't be put in a shared space where it gets in everyone's way.
t1-5.why:
The higher the state lives, the larger the subtree that re-renders on every update. If a modal's isOpen lives in App, opening the modal re-renders the entire app. If that state lives in Modal, only the modal re-renders.

In an interview say: "First I push the state down; memo is the last resort". Memo has its own cost, while colocation is free.
pros: Zero-cost optimization: no memo, no library
The component becomes portable and can be moved anywhere
The code is easy to read because state sits next to where it is used
cons: If you later need it in two places, you have to lift it
Prop drilling can increase in deep trees
It doesn't work for global concerns (auth, theme)
gotchas: Put filter, tab, page and search query in the URL, not in useState. It makes them shareable and back-button friendly
Lift state only when siblings actually need it, not before
In an interview say "first colocation, then composition, finally memo". That is the right order
terms: keeping state next to where it is used
moving state up to the nearest common parent
where: answer with colocation first and memo later

t1-6.what:
Definition: Accessibility isn't something you bolt on later; it is part of the component's design. Every widget needs four things:

  1. Semantic HTML: <button>, <nav>, <dialog> (not an onClick on a div)
  2. Keyboard: Tab, Enter/Space, Arrow keys, Escape, Home/End
  3. ARIA: role, state (aria-expanded), relationships (aria-controls)
  4. Focus management: where focus goes when the widget opens, and where it returns when it closes
t1-6.why:
Mentioning a11y in an interview signals seniority, because few candidates do. It matters in practice too: a <div onClick> can't be activated with the keyboard, screen readers don't announce it as a control, and the Enter key does nothing. A <button> gives you all three for free.

The best rule is to choose the correct HTML element first. That gets you half of accessibility. Add ARIA only when HTML has no suitable element (tabs, combobox).
pros: Semantic HTML gives you half the work for free
Keyboard users, screen reader users and power users all benefit
You stand out immediately in an interview
cons: Testing needs a real screen reader (NVDA/VoiceOver)
Incorrect ARIA is worse than no ARIA
Focus management has many edge cases
gotchas: The first rule of ARIA: no ARIA is better than bad ARIA. Choose the right HTML element first
aria-label overrides the native text, so the screen reader reads it instead of the visible text
Never remove the focus outline. Style it with :focus-visible instead of hiding it
terms: Accessible Rich Internet Applications: extra semantics for assistive technology
only one element in a group is tab-focusable; the rest are reached with arrow keys
keeping focus confined inside a modal
where: mentioning a11y is a signal of seniority
WCAG is mandatory at large companies

t2-1.what:
Definition: 10,000 rows of DOM will kill the browser. With virtualization, only the ~20 visible rows get DOM nodes, and the scrollbar's height is faked with a spacer.

In a design round this is the standard answer for a "large list", but saying it alone isn't enough. You also have to state its tradeoffs.
t2-1.why:
Every DOM node costs memory and layout time. 10k rows can freeze the browser for 5-10 seconds. In a virtualized list only about 20 nodes exist, so 10k rows and 1M rows run at roughly the same speed.

In an interview, add this: virtualization isn't free. Ctrl+F doesn't find off-screen text, the content is invisible to SEO, and variable-height rows need measuring. So don't apply it to lists of up to a couple of hundred rows.
pros: Performance is almost independent of list size
Memory usage is very low
Scrolling stays smooth even with 1M rows
cons: Browser find-in-page and SEO both stop working
The scroll position can jump with variable-height rows
Accessibility needs extra work, since screen readers don't see the full list
gotchas: Mention the tradeoffs in an interview. Just saying "we'll virtualize" sounds junior
If estimateSize is wrong for variable heights, the scrollbar jumps. Use measureElement
Don't virtualize up to ~200 rows. A plain list works fine
terms: rendering only the visible items into the DOM
extra rows rendered just outside the window to keep scrolling smooth
each row has a different height, which is the hardest case

t2-2.what:
Definition: There are three ways to present large datasets: numbered pagination, infinite scroll and a load more button. On the backend there are two approaches: offset and cursor.

In a design round these are two separate decisions, and you will be asked about both.
t2-2.why:
The offset bug that comes up in every interview: you are viewing page 1 and a new item is added at the top. When you request page 2, the item that was last on page 1 has slid down and shows up at the top of page 2. You see it again. If an item is deleted instead, one item gets skipped.

A cursor avoids this because you send an identifier rather than a position: "the items after this id". That is why real-time feeds (Twitter, Slack) use cursors.
pros: Cursor: consistent results and fast on the DB (index seek, no OFFSET scan)
Numbered: users can jump around, URLs are shareable, the back button works
Load more: the benefits of infinite scroll, plus an accessible footer
cons: Cursor: "go to page 5" isn't possible
Infinite scroll: scroll position is lost on back navigation and the footer is unreachable
Offset: slow on large offsets (OFFSET 100000 scans 100k rows)
gotchas: Offset drift is a favorite interview question. Have a duplicate/skip example ready
With infinite scroll, handle scroll restoration yourself, otherwise the back button sends the user to the top
Use IntersectionObserver, not a scroll listener. Scroll events can fire up to 60 times per second
terms: page=3&limit=20, which is OFFSET 40 in SQL
after=<last-item-id>, meaning "the next items after this one"

where: a Load more button, with the footer still reachable

t2-3.what:
Definition: The data table is a classic design round because it covers everything: sorting, filtering, pagination, virtualization, column resize, row selection, sticky header and responsiveness.

The most important decision is server-side or client-side? Up to about 1,000 rows, do it on the client; above that, on the server.
t2-3.why:
In interviews, people jump straight into implementation. The better approach is to ask about scale first: "How many rows? 100 or 1,000,000?" The whole architecture depends on the answer:

  • <1,000 rows: everything on the client, sort/filter in memory, no API
  • >1,000: server-side sorting/filtering/pagination, the client only displays
  • >10,000 visible: add virtualization too
pros: A headless library (TanStack Table) provides the logic for free, and the styling is entirely yours
Server-side processing removes the dataset size limit
keepPreviousData prevents flicker when sorting or changing pages
cons: Every interaction on the server-side approach costs a network round trip
Column resize combined with virtualization is quite complex
Tables are inherently poor on mobile and need a different layout
gotchas: First ask "how many rows?" The entire design depends on it
Track row selection by id, not by index, because indexes change after sorting
Implement the sticky header with CSS (position:sticky), not with a JS scroll listener

the header stays pinned at the top while scrolling
a logic library supplies the functionality and you write the markup (TanStack Table)

"design a data table" is a standard question

t2-4.what:
Definition: Every data-driven UI has four states, not three:

  1. Loading: a skeleton (not a spinner, if the shape is known)
  2. Error: what happened, plus a retry button
  3. Empty: two separate cases, "there was never any data" and "nothing matched the filter"
  4. Success: the actual content

Calling out all four in a design round shows maturity. A junior only thinks about loading and success.
t2-4.why:
An empty state needs two forms because the user's need differs. "No orders yet" → they need a button to start shopping. "This filter found nothing" → they need a button to clear the filter. A single "No data" message is useless in both cases.

A skeleton also beats a spinner because it reserves the layout. The page doesn't jump when the content arrives (CLS = 0).
pros: A skeleton gives zero CLS, so the page doesn't jump
A proper empty state tells the user the next step
A retry button lets a transient network error heal itself
cons: Four states means four UI pieces to build and maintain
The skeleton must be kept in sync with the content
Too many skeletons make the page feel "busy"
gotchas: Build two separate empty states. "Never had data" and "nothing matched the filter" are completely different
Make the skeleton the same height as a real row, otherwise the page shifts when content appears
Always provide a retry in the error state. Without it, the error is a dead end
terms: a grey placeholder matching the shape of the content
the UI shown when there is no data at all
Cumulative Layout Shift: the page jumping when content arrives
where: each widget has its own four states

t2-5.what:
Definition: In an optimistic update you assume the server will say yes. You update the UI immediately and send the request in the background. If it fails, you revert to the previous state.

Three things are required: (1) save the previous state, (2) roll back on failure, (3) reconcile with the server afterwards.
t2-5.analogy: Asking a friend to lend you $20. You assume they'll say yes and start making plans. If they refuse, you cancel the plans, but in the meantime you saved time.
t2-5.why:
A Like button that waits 300 ms for the server feels sluggish. With optimistic updates the app feels "instant", which is the biggest lever for perceived performance.

But not every action should be optimistic. In an interview say: "optimistic only when the chance of failure is low and rollback is cheap." Like, star, reorder: yes. Payment, delete, checkout: never.
pros: The app feels instant, the biggest lever for perceived performance
A huge difference on slow networks
A first step toward offline-first
cons: Rollback logic must be written for every mutation
Race conditions on rapid clicking
The user may briefly see an incorrect state
gotchas: In onMutate, always call cancelQueries. Otherwise an older in-flight response can overwrite your optimistic update
Never make irreversible actions (payment, delete) optimistic
Show a toast when you roll back. Silently reverting confuses the user
terms: changing the UI before the server responds
restoring the previous state when the server request fails
sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once

t2-6.what:
Definition: An API often returns nested data, where each post contains the full author object. If one author has 20 posts, that object sits in memory 20 times. If the author's name changes, you have to update it in 20 places.

Normalization flattens the data into { posts: {id: post}, users: {id: user} } and keeps only an authorId in each post.
t2-6.analogy: Writing the full address in every row of an Excel sheet, versus creating a separate "customers" sheet and storing only the customer ID in each row. If the address changes, you update it in one place instead of 500 rows.
t2-6.why:
This comes up in interviews when an entity appears in multiple places: the user's name on every chat message, the author on every feed post. Without normalization, a single update can leave half the UI stale.

It isn't needed everywhere. With a cache like React Query, a simple invalidate is often enough. Use normalization when the entity appears in multiple places, when you need real-time updates, or when you need offline support.
pros: One entity, one place, so updates are never partial
Lower memory use (no duplicate objects)
Applying real-time patches becomes trivial
cons: Reading requires joining data (selectors)
Boilerplate: you write both normalize and denormalize
Complete overkill for small apps
gotchas: Don't normalize everywhere. React Query's invalidate is often enough
Keep the order separate (feed: string[]) and don't rely on object key order
A library like Normalizr works, but a 30-line custom function is usually enough
terms: flattening nested data into "id → object" maps
nested tree data, as the API returns it
each entity's data exists in exactly one place
where: a single update shows up across the whole app

t3-1.what:
Definition: Both reduce the rate of rapid events, but in different ways:

  • Debounce: "do nothing until it stops". Use it for search input.
  • Throttle: "keep going, but at most once every 200ms". Use it for scroll, resize and mouse-move.

A search box needs debounce because firing an API call on every keystroke wastes resources and exhausts rate limits.
t3-1.analogy: An elevator door. Debounce: if someone is coming, keep waiting, and close only after nobody has arrived for 3 seconds. Throttle: close once every 10 seconds, no matter how many people arrive.
t3-1.why:
In a design round, saying only "we'll add debounce" is a half answer. The complete answer has three parts:

  1. Debounce: reduces network calls (typically 300ms)
  2. Cancel/abort: stop the previous in-flight request, otherwise an out-of-order response shows stale results
  3. Cache: if the same query comes again, skip the network

Debounce alone does not fix a race condition. That is a separate problem.
pros: Network calls drop by 10-20x
Saves both rate limit and server load
Abort eliminates the out-of-order results bug
cons: Debounce increases perceived latency (an extra 300ms)
A wrong delay makes the UI either laggy or spammy
Debounce alone doesn't fix a race condition
gotchas: Mention all three: debounce + abort + cache. Saying only debounce is a half answer
Keep the debounced function in useMemo/useRef, otherwise a new timer is created on every render
Don't debounce scroll. Use throttle there, otherwise nothing happens while the user is scrolling
terms: wait for the events to stop, then run N ms after the last one
rate limit: run at most once every N ms
run at the end of the window or at the start

t3-2.what:
Definition: Autocomplete is the most common design-round question because it covers so much: debounce, caching, race conditions, keyboard navigation, ARIA, virtualization and highlighting.

A complete answer has 5 layers: input handling → network → cache → keyboard/ARIA → rendering.
t3-2.why:
The interviewer checks how many layers you remember. Most people stop after debounce + fetch. These are the details that make you stand out:

  • Keyboard: Arrow up/down, Enter, Escape, Home/End
  • ARIA: role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant, with focus staying on the input
  • Minimum length (2 chars), plus empty and no-results states
  • Highlighting: bold the matched portion, and escape user input (XSS)
pros: Typing the same query again gets an instant response thanks to the cache
Keyboard navigation means power users don't need a mouse
A minimum length prevents unnecessary API calls
cons: Many edge cases: blur, click, escape, IME input
On mobile, the keyboard and dropdown compete for space
If results exceed 1,000, you also need virtualization
gotchas: Call preventDefault on onMouseDown, otherwise the input blurs and the click isn't registered
Keep focus on the input. Don't focus the list item; use aria-activedescendant
Escape user input when highlighting, otherwise you open an XSS vector

t3-3.what:
Definition: Architecting a large form comes down to three decisions:

  1. Where state lives: controlled (re-renders on every keystroke) or uncontrolled (via RHF, refs)
  2. When to validate: onChange / onBlur / onSubmit, and where the schema lives
  3. How to show errors: below the field, a summary on top, or both

The design-round answer: uncontrolled + schema validation + onBlur first, onChange after the first error.
t3-3.why:
With 30 controlled fields, 30 components re-render on every keystroke. RHF keeps fields uncontrolled, so typing causes zero re-renders, and it renders only when an error appears.

Validation timing is a big part of UX. Don't start with onChange: the user types "m" and immediately sees "invalid email", which is irritating. The right pattern is to validate on onBlur first; once an error appears, validate on onChange so the error disappears as soon as it's fixed.
pros: Even large forms are fast when uncontrolled
Types and validation come from a single schema
You can map server errors onto fields
cons: Custom components (MUI, Radix) need to be wrapped with Controller
Cross-field validation (password match) takes a bit of extra work
Async validation (is the username available?) can have race conditions
gotchas: Don't start validating on onChange. Start with onTouched (blur), then switch to onChange
Provide defaultValues, or you'll get an "uncontrolled to controlled" warning
Connect the error to the input with aria-describedby, otherwise screen readers won't know about the error

writing the rules in one place (zod/yup)

t4-1.what:
Definition: There are three ways to get real-time data to the client:

  • Polling — the client asks repeatedly. Simple, but latency is as long as the interval and most requests are wasted.
  • SSE — the server pushes data in one direction over plain HTTP, with auto-reconnect built in.
  • WebSocket — two-way, full duplex. The most powerful option, and the most infrastructure work.
t4-1.why:
In an interview, don’t default to WebSocket. That’s a junior signal. Let the requirements pick the answer:

  • Does the client need to send data too (chat, cursors, collaboration)? Use WebSocket.
  • Does it only need to receive (notifications, live scores, AI token streams)? Use SSE: simple, cheap, and it reconnects automatically.
  • Are updates rare (every 30 seconds)? Use polling and stop there.

The key point about SSE is that it uses normal HTTP, so proxies, CDNs, and auth work without extra configuration.

WebSocket: lowest latency, two-way
Polling: no extra infrastructure, and it rarely fails
cons: WebSocket: sticky sessions on the load balancer, scaling, and reconnect logic are all on you
SSE: HTTP/1.1 limits browsers to 6 connections per domain
Polling: wasteful load on the server

SSE hits the 6-connection limit on HTTP/1.1, but not on HTTP/2
WebSocket needs sticky sessions on the load balancer, so be sure to mention it

t4-2.what:
Definition: Connections will break: the WiFi changes, you enter a tunnel, the laptop sleeps, the server deploys. The real question is not if, but how you reconnect.

You need four things: (1) exponential backoff with jitter, (2) a way to fill the gap of missed messages, (3) an offline queue, and (4) a visible connection status for the user.
t4-2.why:
Thundering herd is the heart of this topic. The server was down for 30 seconds and comes back, and now 50,000 clients reconnect at once and knock it over again. Jitter is the fix: if each client waits a random amount of time, the load spreads out.

In an interview, say "exponential backoff with jitter". It’s much stronger than just saying backoff.
pros: Jitter prevents a reconnect storm on the server.
An offline queue ensures the user's message isn't lost.
Since/Last-Event-ID fills in missed messages.
cons: It requires managing a lot of state.
Filling the gap needs message history on the server.
It’s hard to test, since you have to simulate the network.
gotchas: Say "exponential backoff WITH JITTER"; plain "backoff" leaves the answer half finished.
Listen to both the online event and visibilitychange so you reconnect immediately when the user returns.
Show the connection status (live / reconnecting / offline). Failing silently is the worst UX.

random variation in the wait time so clients don’t all retry together
thousands of clients reconnecting the moment the server comes back

t4-3.what:
Definition: When a user sends a chat message, it should appear on screen immediately, without waiting for the server to confirm. This takes three steps:

  1. Create a temp id (uuid) and insert the message into the list right away with status sending
  2. When the server responds, replace the temp id with the real id
  3. If it fails, set status failed and show a retry button. Never delete the message
t4-3.why:
This differs from a plain optimistic update because of an identity problem: the client creates one id, the server creates another, and the same message can come back over the WebSocket (an echo). Without a temp-id mapping, you get a duplicate.

A failed message should never be removed. The user typed it, and that effort matters. A failed state plus retry is the right UX.

t4-4.what:
Definition: Presence (online/offline) and typing indicators are ephemeral data. They aren’t stored in the DB; they live only in memory or Redis with a short TTL.

There are two standard patterns: presence via heartbeat + TTL, and typing via a throttled event + auto-expire.
t4-4.why:
A naive typing indicator sends an event on every keystroke, which is about 60 messages per minute per user. In a room of 50 people that’s 3,000 messages a minute just for "typing". The right approach is to throttle (one "typing" event every 3 seconds) and use auto-expire on the receiving side (clear the indicator after 5 seconds).

Auto-expire is needed because a "stopped typing" event can get lost (the user disconnects, the network drops), and the indicator would otherwise stay stuck forever.

t4-6.what:
Definition: What happens when two people change the same thing at the same time? There are three strategies:

  • LWW — the later timestamp wins. Simple, but the other person’s work silently disappears.
  • OT — transform each operation against the other. Powerful, but it needs a central server and is very hard to implement.
  • CRDT — design the data structure so merges always converge to the same result. No central server needed, but it uses more memory.
t4-6.analogy: Two people are writing in the same Google Doc. With LWW, whichever save happened last is kept and the other is lost. With a CRDT, both people’s words stay where they were written and nothing is lost.
t4-6.why:
In an interview you’re not expected to implement a CRDT yourself. What you should do is:

  1. Spot the conflict: "what if two people edit at the same time?"
  2. Pick the right strategy for the product. LWW is fine for a form field, not for a text editor
  3. Know the library names: Yjs (CRDT) and Automerge

There’s also a practical fallback: field-level locking ("Riya is editing this field"). It’s enough for many business apps and takes about a day to build.

Version check: easy to implement, and data never disappears silently
Field locking: the simplest option, and clearly visible to the user
cons: CRDT: memory overhead and a heavy mental model
OT: needs a central server and is very hard to implement
LWW: data disappears silently and the user never notices
gotchas: Don’t implement a CRDT yourself; use Yjs or Automerge and say so in the interview
Use the server timestamp for LWW, not the client’s, since client clocks are unreliable
Silent overwrite is the worst option; showing a conflict dialog on a 409 response is enough
terms: whichever write arrives last wins: simple, but data can be lost
Operational Transform: the older method used by Google Docs

t5-1.what:
Definition: SPA routing architecture comes down to four decisions:

  1. Code splitting — each route gets its own chunk (lazy + Suspense)
  2. Data loading — in a loader before render, or inside the component
  3. Nested layouts — sidebar and nav don’t re-render during navigation
  4. Prefetch — load the next route on hover or when it enters the viewport
t5-1.why:
The core interview point is the waterfall. In the old pattern: route match → chunk download → component render → useEffect → data fetch. That’s three sequential steps, say 300ms + 200ms + 400ms.

With loader-based routing, the router knows which data it needs the moment the route matches, so the chunk and the data load in parallel. In nested routes, all matching loaders run together instead of one after another.

State in a nested layout is preserved across navigation
Prefetch makes navigation feel instant
cons: Over-splitting means every navigation triggers a new request

Hooks can’t be used inside a data loader

Prefetch on hover, but on mobile use touchstart because hover never fires
Route-level splitting is the biggest win, so don’t start with component-level splitting

t5-2.what:
Definition: "State management" isn’t one thing. It’s four separate problems, each with its own tool:

  1. Server state → React Query / SWR / RTK Query
  2. URL state → searchParams
  3. Global client state → Zustand / Jotai / Context
  4. Local state → useState / useReducer

In a design round, naming these four is the real answer, not "I’ll use Redux".
t5-2.why:
About 90% of the "pain of state management" comes from treating server state like client state. Server data needs caching, refetching, deduplication, and stale detection. Redux provides none of that, so people write it by hand and the store grows to 5,000 lines.

Once server state and URL state are split out, the remaining global client state is often so small that a 30-line Zustand store is enough.

Each tool does its own job best

Don’t copy server data into the store, or you’ll have two sources of truth
Context is not a state manager; it’s a dependency injection tool

t5-3.what:
Definition: Frontend auth has three parts:

  1. Where to store the token — an httpOnly cookie (safer) vs localStorage (can be stolen via XSS)
  2. How to refresh — on a 401, run only one refresh and make all pending requests wait for it
  3. Authorization — what to show (UI) vs what to allow (server)
t5-3.why:
The most important line to say in an interview: frontend authorization is only UX, not security. Hiding a button doesn’t protect any API, because a user can send the request from DevTools. The real check always happens on the server.

On token storage: a token in localStorage can be stolen via XSS. An httpOnly cookie can’t be read by JavaScript, but you then need SameSite=Strict or a CSRF token to defend against CSRF. Mentioning this tradeoff is essential.

Single-flight refresh prevents a refresh storm
Cross-tab logout keeps security consistent
cons: Cookies need separate CSRF protection

Keeping permissions on the client increases payload size

Definition: An error boundary strategy is about where you place boundaries so that one crashing widget doesn’t take down the whole app.

There are three levels: root (the final safety net), route (one page breaks, navigation still works), and widget (one chart breaks, the rest of the dashboard keeps working).

Since React 16, an uncaught error unmounts the entire app, leaving a white screen. A boundary only at the root swaps the white screen for "Something went wrong", but the user’s work is still lost.

t5-6.what:
Definition: i18n is more than translating strings. It has five parts:

  1. Strings — keys + translation files, lazy-loaded per locale
  2. Plurals & gender — ICU format (every language has different rules)
  3. Formatting — dates, numbers, currency (Intl API)
  4. RTL — layout mirroring for Arabic/Hebrew
  5. Locale detection — URL, cookie, or Accept-Language
t5-6.why:
The most common mistake is string concatenation. "You have " + n + " items" can’t be translated, because word order differs between languages and so do plural rules: Russian has four plural forms and Arabic has six. That’s why ICU format exists.

Another mistake is shipping every language in one bundle. 20 languages × 50 KB = 1 MB, but each user needs only 50 KB. Lazy-load per locale instead.
